title: Rebuild what matters
summary: Fill the space you free up with actions that mean something to you.

vacuum.title: Plan what will take its place
vacuum.paragraph1: Removing a habit frees up time, attention, and sometimes a way of soothing a difficult evening. If nothing takes that place, it tends to be filled by whatever is most reachable.
vacuum.paragraph2: A plan made only of prohibitions can therefore run out of steam: it describes what you no longer do, never what you do.
vacuum.paragraph3: So the useful question is not only “how do I stop?” but “what do I put there, concretely, on Tuesday at 10 p.m.?”
vacuum.keyPoint1: Write your plan as actions, not only as bans.
vacuum.keyPoint2: Plan for the exact moment that frees up.
vacuum.keyPoint3: Make the alternative easy to reach.

activation.title: Act before you feel like it
activation.paragraph1: We often wait for motivation before acting. Behavioral activation proposes the reverse order: schedule activities, then observe that mood follows, at least partly.
activation.paragraph2: A meta-analysis in depression observed that these structured activity programs produced effects comparable to other established psychological treatments. This work concerns depression, not this habit specifically, but the principle remains informative.
activation.paragraph3: In practice: put the activity in your week like an appointment, without waiting to feel like it on the day.

values.title: Actions connected to what you care about
values.paragraph1: An activity connected to something that matters to you—a relationship, a skill, your health, or something you create—may be easier to choose again.
values.paragraph2: Acceptance and commitment therapies work explicitly in this direction, and reviews report effects across various mental health problems. A small preliminary study also applied this approach to problematic online pornography use: the results observed in six participants were encouraging, but still need confirmation in controlled trials.
values.paragraph3: A good starting question: if this difficulty took up less room, what would you spend that time on?
values.keyPoint1: Tie each action to a value, not to a performance.
values.keyPoint2: Choose an activity that fits you.
values.keyPoint3: Aim for meaning, not for being busy.

small.title: Small enough for a bad day
small.paragraph1: An alternative is only useful if it stays possible when you are tired, irritated, or alone. Those are exactly the states in which you will need it.
small.paragraph2: You can plan two formats: a full version for good days, and a minimal version for the others. A short walk rather than a workout, one page read rather than a chapter.
small.paragraph3: The minimal version is not a failed full version. It is what keeps the whole plan from stopping.

people.title: Not carrying it all alone
people.paragraph1: Keeping this difficulty entirely to yourself can reinforce isolation or shame and make support less accessible when it would help.
people.paragraph2: You do not have to tell everything to create connection. A regularly shared activity can already provide company and support, without requiring you to explain the subject.
people.paragraph3: If you do choose to talk to someone, choose a person from whom you expect support, not an assessment of your worth.

reflectionPrompt: Which activity would you like to take up more room in your week?
